newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan asks FAA for tighter checks by Northwest Air.
newsitem.headline: Japan asks FAA for tighter checks by Northwest Air.

text.p: Japan's Transport Ministry said on Friday it has asked the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to instruct Northwest Airlines Corp to improve its maintenance operations in Japan.

A ministry official said Northwest accounted for 13 percent of total flights arriving and departing from Tokyo's Narita airport, but incidents of mechanical trouble involving Northwest were some 40 percent of all such incidents last year.

"Narita has only one runway, and when such incidents occur the runway has to be temporarily closed, harming airport operations...so we have asked the FAA to take preventive measures regarding these incidents," the official said.
The official said the transport ministry's request did not go so far as to mean that that the ministry had doubts about Northwest's safety operations.

"Some Japanese airlines have temporarily had times where they had many incidents of irregular flight operations and we instructed them individually to take preventive measures -- it is not as if we are picking on Northwest," he said.
The official said incidents of irregular flight operations included flying back to Narita after take-off and emergency landings because of engine trouble.
The ministry said 20 of 51 incidents at Narita in 1996 involved Northwest and that the airline had an incident rate of one in every 800 flights, more than double the average.
Northwest said on Thursday that suggestions that its aircraft maintenance operations in Japan had problems were unfair.

"Of those 20 incidents that the airport authorities in Narita cite for Northwest in 1996, some were as minor as a plugged lavatory drain, which we elected to go back to Narita for," said Doug Killien, Northwest's director of international communications, speaking at its headquarters in Minneapolis.

"Under FAA regulations for U.S. carriers, anytime we make a precautionary engine shutdown or decide to return, we need to declare an emergency," he said. "That's not the case for Japanese airlines, necessarily."
Northwest is the world's fourth-largest airline and has the second-largest presence among all carriers in Narita, with some 17,000 flights a year out of the main Japanese airport.
